claim: Homologous recombination involving sister chromatids is the most accurate, and thus most frequently used, form of recombination-mediated DNA repair.
source: Homologous recombination involving sister chromatids is the most accurate, and thus most frequently used, form of recombination-mediated DNA repair.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus about homologous recombination.

claim: Sister chromatid recombination does not result in a change in DNA sequence, making recombination between sister chromatids difficult to detect.
source: Despite its importance, sister chromatid recombination is not easily studied because it does not result in a change in DNA sequence, making recombination between sister chromatids difficult to detect.
evidence: This explains a known technical challenge in studying sister chromatid recombination based on the nature of the process.

claim: Strand-seq is a novel DNA template strand sequencing technique that can be used to map sister chromatid exchange (SCE) events genome-wide in single cells.
source: We have previously developed a novel DNA template strand sequencing technique, called Strand-seq, that can be used to map sister chromatid exchange (SCE) events genome-wide in single cells.
evidence: The authors reference their previous development of the Strand-seq technique.

claim: An increase in the rate of SCE is an indicator of elevated recombination activity and of genome instability, which is a hallmark of cancer.
source: An increase in the rate of SCE is an indicator of elevated recombination activity and of genome instability, which is a hallmark of cancer.
evidence: This statement draws on established knowledge about the relationship between SCE, genome instability, and cancer.

claim: This study adapted Strand-seq to detect SCE in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: In this study, we have adapted Strand-seq to detect SCE in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
evidence: The authors describe their methodological adaptation as a primary contribution of the study.

claim: Most spontaneous SCE events in wild-type cells are not due to the repair of DNA double-strand breaks.
source: We provide the first quantifiable evidence that most spontaneous SCE events in wild-type cells are not due to the repair of DNA double-strand breaks.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on their experimental data and analysis.

claim: Mutations in many HR genes are linked to a number of human diseases, especially various types of cancer.
source: Homologous recombination (HR) is indispensable for the maintenance of genome integrity, and mutations in many HR genes are linked to a number of human diseases, especially various types of cancer (Prakash et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Prakash et al., 2015.

claim: HR is characterized as a major pathway to repair DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs).
source: HR is characterized as a major pathway to repair DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs), and can occur between any two homologous sequences, such as sister chromatids, homologous chromosomes, or homologous sequences located at different genomic loci (Jasin and Rothstein, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jasin and Rothstein, 2013.

claim: HR can occur between any two homologous sequences, such as sister chromatids, homologous chromosomes, or homologous sequences located at different genomic loci.
source: HR is characterized as a major pathway to repair DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs), and can occur between any two homologous sequences, such as sister chromatids, homologous chromosomes, or homologous sequences located at different genomic loci (Jasin and Rothstein, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jasin and Rothstein, 2013.

claim: HR results in a unidirectional transfer of genetic information from one DNA molecule to another (i.e. gene conversion) and/or a reciprocal exchange of genetic information between the two DNA molecules (i.e. a crossover).
source: HR results in a unidirectional transfer of genetic information from one DNA molecule to another (i.e. gene conversion) and/or a reciprocal exchange of genetic information between the two DNA molecules (i.e. a crossover).
evidence: This describes the known outcomes of homologous recombination.

claim: A crossover involving two homologous chromosomes can cause loss of heterozygosity, which is a common occurrence in cancer.
source: A crossover involving two homologous chromosomes can cause loss of heterozygosity, which is a common occurrence in cancer, while a crossover involving homologous sequences located at different genomic loci will result in chromosomal rearrangements, such as deletions, inversions, and translocations, which have been linked to a variety of human diseases (Kong et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kong et al., 2011.

claim: A crossover involving homologous sequences located at different genomic loci will result in chromosomal rearrangements, such as deletions, inversions, and translocations, which have been linked to a variety of human diseases.
source: A crossover involving two homologous chromosomes can cause loss of heterozygosity, which is a common occurrence in cancer, while a crossover involving homologous sequences located at different genomic loci will result in chromosomal rearrangements, such as deletions, inversions, and translocations, which have been linked to a variety of human diseases (Kong et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kong et al., 2011.

claim: In mitotic cells, HR is biased towards noncrossovers.
source: Thus, in mitotic cells, HR is biased towards noncrossovers, and HR involving identical sister chromatids, referred to as sister chromatid recombination (SCR), is preferred (Kadyk and Hartwell, 1992; Nassif et al., 1994; Johnson and Jasin, 2000; Virgin et al., 2001; Stark and Jasin, 2003), in part because a crossover during SCR should not lead to a change in DNA sequence.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: HR involving identical sister chromatids, referred to as sister chromatid recombination (SCR), is preferred in mitotic cells.
source: Thus, in mitotic cells, HR is biased towards noncrossovers, and HR involving identical sister chromatids, referred to as sister chromatid recombination (SCR), is preferred (Kadyk and Hartwell, 1992; Nassif et al., 1994; Johnson and Jasin, 2000; Virgin et al., 2001; Stark and Jasin, 2003), in part because a crossover during SCR should not lead to a change in DNA sequence.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: A crossover during SCR should not lead to a change in DNA sequence.
source: Thus, in mitotic cells, HR is biased towards noncrossovers, and HR involving identical sister chromatids, referred to as sister chromatid recombination (SCR), is preferred (Kadyk and Hartwell, 1992; Nassif et al., 1994; Johnson and Jasin, 2000; Virgin et al., 2001; Stark and Jasin, 2003), in part because a crossover during SCR should not lead to a change in DNA sequence.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the nature of identical sister chromatids.

claim: The mechanistic details of SCE and HR have been best studied using genetic assays in the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: The mechanistic details of SCE and HR have been best studied using genetic assays in the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Symington et al., 2014), though these assays are limited in several ways.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Symington et al., 2014.

claim: Perfect, or 'equal', chromosomal SCE events cannot be detected genetically.
source: First, perfect, or 'equal', chromosomal SCE events cannot be detected genetically, so most SCE assays measure 'unequal' SCE events, requiring recombination between misaligned sister chromatids.
evidence: This describes a limitation of genetic assays based on the nature of equal SCE events.

claim: Using a plasmid-based assay that creates a DSB on one of the two sister plasmids after DNA replication, equal SCE was found to occur much more frequently than unequal SCE.
source: However, using a plasmid-based assay that creates a DSB on one of the two sister plasmids after DNA replication, equal SCE was found to occur much more frequently than unequal SCE (González-Barrera et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to González-Barrera et al., 2003.

claim: An often-used approach for detecting unequal SCE involves using two overlapping segments of a reporter gene in a tail-to-head configuration.
source: Second, an often-used approach for detecting unequal SCE involves using two overlapping segments of a reporter gene in a tail-to-head configuration (Fasullo and Davis, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fasullo and Davis, 1987.

claim: The generation of a full-length reporter gene can result from an unequal SCE event, but it can also result from a long-tract gene conversion event, which does not involve a crossover.
source: The generation of a full-length reporter gene can result from an unequal SCE event, but it can also result from a long-tract gene conversion event, which does not involve a crossover.
evidence: This describes a limitation of reporter gene assays based on the ambiguity of outcomes.

claim: These two outcomes can be distinguished by analysis of sectored colonies, but this additional analysis is often not performed.
source: These two outcomes can be distinguished by analysis of sectored colonies (Kadyk and Hartwell, 1992), but this additional analysis is often not performed.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kadyk and Hartwell, 1992, and describes a methodological limitation.

claim: Introduction of reporter cassettes may disrupt the native chromatin environment, which could affect HR at the locus.
source: Introduction of such 'reporter cassettes' may disrupt the native chromatin environment, which could affect HR at the locus.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential artifacts of reporter cassette insertion.

claim: Most genetic assays rely on the outgrowth of a recombined cell, thus recombination events that lead to a reduction in cell proliferation capacity will be underrepresented, or left uncharacterized.
source: Lastly, most genetic assays rely on the outgrowth of a recombined cell. Thus, recombination events that lead to a reduction in cell proliferation capacity will be underrepresented, or left uncharacterized.
evidence: This describes a selection bias inherent in genetic assays.

claim: Strand-seq is capable of detecting SCE events genome-wide in single cells.
source: To alleviate these limitations, we previously developed a DNA template strand sequencing technique, called Strand-seq, which is capable of detecting SCE events genome-wide in single cells (Falconer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Falconer et al., 2012.

claim: In Strand-seq, cells are allowed to divide once in the presence of bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU), a synthetic analogue of thymidine.
source: In Strand-seq, cells are allowed to divide once in the presence of bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU), a synthetic analogue of thymidine.
evidence: This describes the Strand-seq methodology.

claim: BrdU gets incorporated into the newly synthesized DNA strands.
source: BrdU gets incorporated into the newly synthesized DNA strands.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of BrdU incorporation in Strand-seq.

claim: Single daughter cells are isolated and the nascent DNA strands are selectively degraded to isolate parental template strands for the construction of directional sequencing libraries.
source: Single daughter cells are isolated and the nascent DNA strands are selectively degraded to isolate parental template strands for the construction of directional sequencing libraries.
evidence: This describes the Strand-seq methodology.

claim: An SCE is revealed by a switch in reads mapping to the Watson strand to reads mapping to the Crick strand, or vice versa.
source: An SCE is revealed by a switch in reads mapping to the Watson strand to reads mapping to the Crick strand, or vice versa (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes how SCE is detected in Strand-seq data, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Strand-seq was originally developed for use with mammalian cells.
source: Strand-seq was originally developed for use with mammalian cells.
evidence: This is a historical statement about the development of Strand-seq.

claim: Since most mammalian cells are diploid, it is not easy to differentiate between an SCE from an interhomolog recombination event.
source: However, since most mammalian cells are diploid, it is not easy to differentiate between an SCE from an interhomolog recombination event.
evidence: This is an inference based on the diploid nature of mammalian cells.

claim: Yeast can be studied in both haploid and diploid states.
source: Yeast, on the other hand, can be studied in both haploid and diploid states, and the molecular details of HR are best known from studies in yeast.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast biology.

claim: The molecular details of HR are best known from studies in yeast.
source: Yeast, on the other hand, can be studied in both haploid and diploid states, and the molecular details of HR are best known from studies in yeast.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast as a model organism for HR studies.

claim: 23% of wild-type cells have at least one SCE.
source: We observe that 23% of wild-type cells have at least one SCE—the first time spontaneous SCEs have been measured and mapped genome-wide in yeast.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data.

claim: This is the first time spontaneous SCEs have been measured and mapped genome-wide in yeast.
source: We observe that 23% of wild-type cells have at least one SCE—the first time spontaneous SCEs have been measured and mapped genome-wide in yeast.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study's findings.

claim: S. cerevisiae cells are unable to 'salvage' nucleosides from the environment.
source: S. cerevisiae cells are unable to 'salvage' nucleosides from the environment, so to perform Strand-seq with yeast cells, we use yeast strains that express both Drosophila melanogaster deoxyribonucleoside kinase (dNK) and the human equilibrative nucleoside transporter (hENT1), allowing cells to take up and incorporate exogenous thymidine and BrdU into their DNA (Vernis, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast biology, supported by a citation to Vernis, 2003.

claim: Yeast strains expressing both Drosophila melanogaster deoxyribonucleoside kinase (dNK) and the human equilibrative nucleoside transporter (hENT1) can take up and incorporate exogenous thymidine and BrdU into their DNA.
source: S. cerevisiae cells are unable to 'salvage' nucleosides from the environment, so to perform Strand-seq with yeast cells, we use yeast strains that express both Drosophila melanogaster deoxyribonucleoside kinase (dNK) and the human equilibrative nucleoside transporter (hENT1), allowing cells to take up and incorporate exogenous thymidine and BrdU into their DNA (Vernis, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vernis, 2003.

claim: CDC21, which encodes thymidylate kinase, is deleted in these strains, forcing them to be entirely dependent upon exogenous thymidine for viability.
source: CDC21, which encodes thymidylate kinase, is also deleted in these strains, forcing them to be entirely dependent upon exogenous thymidine for viability.
evidence: This describes the genetic modification of the strains used in the study.

claim: When grown in the presence of BrdU, these strains do not show any cell cycle delay or DNA damage checkpoint activation during the first cell cycle.
source: When grown in the presence of BrdU, these strains do not show any cell cycle delay or DNA damage checkpoint activation during the first cell cycle (Vernis, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vernis, 2003.

claim: There is no significant difference in Rad52 focus formation after 90 min of growth in BrdU-containing medium, suggesting that BrdU does not stimulate SCE.
source: In addition, we see no significant difference in Rad52 focus formation, a sensitive indicator of recombination activity (Lisby et al., 2001), after 90 min of growth in BrdU-containing medium, suggesting that BrdU does not stimulate SCE (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1, with citation to Lisby et al., 2001.

claim: Rad52 focus formation is a sensitive indicator of recombination activity.
source: In addition, we see no significant difference in Rad52 focus formation, a sensitive indicator of recombination activity (Lisby et al., 2001), after 90 min of growth in BrdU-containing medium, suggesting that BrdU does not stimulate SCE (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lisby et al., 2001.

claim: BrdU incorporation does not induce SCE in human cells, at least during the first two cell divisions, as varying the concentration of BrdU in the culture medium does not affect the frequency of SCE.
source: Although we cannot exclude the possibility that BrdU incorporation causes DNA damage that induces SCE in a manner that does not elicit a DNA damage checkpoint response or Rad52 focus formation, these findings are in line with our recently reported observation that BrdU incorporation also does not induce SCE in human cells, at least during the first two cell divisions, as varying the concentration of BrdU in the culture medium does not affect the frequency of SCE (van Wietmarschen and Lansdorp, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to van Wietmarschen and Lansdorp, 2016.

claim: 218 wild-type Strand-seq libraries were sequenced and a total of 57 SCE events were observed, which equates to 0.26 SCE events per cell.
source: We sequenced Strand-seq libraries derived from 218 wild-type cells and observed a total of 57 SCE events, which equates to 0.26 SCE events per cell (Figure 2A, Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data, shown in Figure 2A and Table 1.

claim: Mutation of BLM, the human homolog of SGS1, increases SCE.
source: Mutation of BLM, the human homolog of SGS1, increases SCE (German et al., 1965; Chaganti et al., 1974; van Wietmarschen and Lansdorp, 2016), and deletion of SGS1 has been reported to increase unequal SCE using two different genetic assays (Onoda et al., 2000; Fasullo and Sun, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Deletion of SGS1 has been reported to increase unequal SCE using two different genetic assays.
source: Mutation of BLM, the human homolog of SGS1, increases SCE (German et al., 1965; Chaganti et al., 1974; van Wietmarschen and Lansdorp, 2016), and deletion of SGS1 has been reported to increase unequal SCE using two different genetic assays (Onoda et al., 2000; Fasullo and Sun, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Onoda et al., 2000 and Fasullo and Sun, 2017.

claim: The evolutionarily conserved Sgs1-Top3-Rmi1 complex is thought to suppress SCE by dissolving a recombination intermediate known as the double Holliday junction (dHJ) in a manner that would result in a non-crossover.
source: The evolutionarily conserved Sgs1-Top3-Rmi1 complex is thought to suppress SCE by dissolving a recombination intermediate known as the double Holliday junction (dHJ; see Figure 1A) in a manner that would result in a non-crossover (Ira et al., 2003; Wu and Hickson, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ira et al., 2003 and Wu and Hickson, 2003, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: An increase in SCE is observed in sgs1∆ cells (p<10−9) using Strand-seq.
source: Consistent with these findings, we observe an increase in SCE in sgs1∆ cells (p<10−9) using Strand-seq (Figure 1D; Figure 2A and B; Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data, shown in Figure 1D, Figure 2A and B, and Table 1.

claim: No SCE events were detected in rad52∆ cells, as expected.
source: In addition, we did not detect any SCE events in rad52∆ cells, as expected (Figure 2A and B; Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data, shown in Figure 2A and B and Table 1.

claim: Spontaneous SCE events per cell is about an order of magnitude greater in human and mouse cells than in wild-type yeast cells.
source: Using previously reported Strand-seq data from mouse embryonic stem cells (Falconer et al., 2012) and human fibroblasts and lymphoblasts (van Wietmarschen and Lansdorp, 2016), we find that spontaneous SCE events per cell is about an order of magnitude greater in human and mouse cells than in wild-type yeast cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on comparison of data from this study with previously published data, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: By plotting the number of SCE events per gigabase of DNA, it is apparent that SCE activity is about 20-fold higher in yeast.
source: However, the human and mouse genomes are much larger than the yeast genome. By plotting the number of SCE events per gigabase of DNA, it is apparent that SCE activity is about 20-fold higher in yeast (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: It is generally thought that yeast is more recombinogenic than mammals, but a direct and quantitative comparison has not been available until now.
source: It is generally thought that yeast is more recombinogenic than mammals, but a direct and quantitative comparison has not been available until now.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study's comparative analysis.

claim: Currently, we are only able to map SCE events to a resolution of approximately 30 kb.
source: Currently, we are only able to map SCE events to a resolution of approximately 30 kb (Figure 3A), which, combined with the modest number of SCE events we have detected so far (57 total from 218 wild-type Strand-seq libraries; Table 1), prevents us from mapping SCE events to specific genomic loci or features.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the current methodology, with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: Multiple SCE events were seen at the ribosomal DNA (rDNA) locus, which is located on chromosome XII and consists of approximately 150 rDNA repeats, each of which is 9.1 kb in size.
source: However, multiple SCE events were seen at the ribosomal DNA (rDNA) locus, which is located on chromosome XII and consists of approximately 150 rDNA repeats, each of which is 9.1 kb in size (the SCE event in the Strand-seq library shown in Figure 1B maps to the rDNA locus).
evidence: This is based on experimental data, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Of the 57 spontaneous SCE events observed in wild-type Strand-seq libraries, 14 were found at the rDNA locus.
source: Of the 57 spontaneous SCE events we observed in our wild-type Strand-seq libraries, 14 were found at the rDNA locus (Table 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data, shown in Table 1.

claim: The rate of spontaneous SCE per gigabase of DNA in the rDNA locus is about threefold higher compared to the rest of the genome.
source: We find that the rate of spontaneous SCE per gigabase of DNA in the rDNA locus is about threefold higher compared to the rest of the genome.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the study's data.

claim: This result was observed both in the presence and absence of Sgs1.
source: This result was observed both in the presence and absence of Sgs1 (Figure 3B), and is likely due to the presence of the replication fork barrier within each rDNA repeat (Labib and Hodgson, 2007).
evidence: This is based on analysis of data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The elevated SCE rate at the rDNA locus is likely due to the presence of the replication fork barrier within each rDNA repeat.
source: This result was observed both in the presence and absence of Sgs1 (Figure 3B), and is likely due to the presence of the replication fork barrier within each rDNA repeat (Labib and Hodgson, 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by a citation to Labib and Hodgson, 2007.

claim: Rad52 has two main biochemical functions: mediating the exchange of replication protein A (RPA) for Rad51 on single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) to promote Rad51-catalyzed strand invasion, and facilitating the annealing of complementary RPA-coated ssDNA.
source: Rad52 has two main biochemical functions. First, Rad52 mediates the exchange of replication protein A (RPA) for Rad51 on single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) to promote Rad51-catalyzed strand invasion (Sung, 1997; New et al., 1998). Second, Rad52 facilitates the annealing of complementary RPA-coated ssDNA, a function that is independent of Rad51 (Mortensen et al., 1996; Shinohara et al., 1998; Sugiyama et al., 1998) and augmented by Rad59 (Petukhova et al., 1999; Davis and Symington, 2001; Wu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing the biochemical functions of Rad52.

claim: The strand annealing function of Rad52 is independent of Rad51.
source: Second, Rad52 facilitates the annealing of complementary RPA-coated ssDNA, a function that is independent of Rad51 (Mortensen et al., 1996; Shinohara et al., 1998; Sugiyama et al., 1998) and augmented by Rad59 (Petukhova et al., 1999; Davis and Symington, 2001; Wu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The strand annealing function of Rad52 is augmented by Rad59.
source: Second, Rad52 facilitates the annealing of complementary RPA-coated ssDNA, a function that is independent of Rad51 (Mortensen et al., 1996; Shinohara et al., 1998; Sugiyama et al., 1998) and augmented by Rad59 (Petukhova et al., 1999; Davis and Symington, 2001; Wu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: rad52-Y66A belongs to a class of rad52 mutants, class C mutants, that are mutated in the evolutionarily conserved N-terminal domain and share a similar phenotype of being proficient for mitotic recombination, but defective in the repair of DSBs.
source: rad52-Y66A belongs to a class of rad52 mutants, class C mutants, that are mutated in the evolutionarily conserved N-terminal domain and share a similar phenotype of being proficient for mitotic recombination, but defective in the repair of DSBs (Mortensen et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mortensen et al., 2002.

claim: An in vitro study of one of the class C mutant proteins, rad52-R70A, indicated that these mutants are defective in strand annealing activity.
source: An in vitro study of one of the class C mutant proteins, rad52-R70A, indicated that these mutants are defective in strand annealing activity (Shi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shi et al., 2009.

claim: SCE is reduced 1.7-fold in rad51∆ cells and 4.5-fold in rad52-Y66A cells (p=0.058 and p<10−4 for rad51∆ and rad52-Y66A, respectively).
source: We find that SCE is reduced 1.7-fold in rad51∆ cells and 4.5-fold in rad52-Y66A cells (p=0.058 and p<10−4 for rad51∆ and rad52-Y66A, respectively; Figure 2A and B; Table 1), indicating that both functions of Rad52 are important for spontaneous SCE, with the strand annealing function being more so.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data, shown in Figure 2A and B and Table 1.

claim: Both functions of Rad52 are important for spontaneous SCE, with the strand annealing function being more so.
source: We find that SCE is reduced 1.7-fold in rad51∆ cells and 4.5-fold in rad52-Y66A cells (p=0.058 and p<10−4 for rad51∆ and rad52-Y66A, respectively; Figure 2A and B; Table 1), indicating that both functions of Rad52 are important for spontaneous SCE, with the strand annealing function being more so.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: The strand annealing activity of Rad52 is important for DSB-induced SCR.
source: This observation is in agreement with previous work indicating that the strand annealing activity of Rad52 is important for DSB-induced SCR (Muñoz-Galván et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Muñoz-Galván et al., 2013.

claim: Using a genetic assay that detects unequal SCE, it was previously reported that Rad51 is not required for spontaneous SCE.
source: Using a genetic assay that detects unequal SCE, it was previously reported that Rad51 is not required for spontaneous SCE (Fasullo et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fasullo et al., 2001.

claim: The effect of rad51∆ and rad52-Y66A on SCE is restricted to outside of the rDNA locus (3.2-fold [p=0.002] and 15-fold [p<10−6] reduction, respectively, compared to wild type).
source: Interestingly, the effect of rad51∆ and rad52-Y66A on SCE is restricted to outside of the rDNA locus (3.2-fold [p=0.002] and 15-fold [p<10−6] reduction, respectively, compared to wild type; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Within the rDNA locus, SCE in rad51∆ and rad52-Y66A is not significantly altered (p=0.48 and p=0.71, respectively).
source: Within the rDNA locus, SCE in rad51∆ and rad52-Y66A is not significantly altered (p=0.48 and p=0.71, respectively).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data.

claim: Spontaneous Holliday junction formation within the rDNA locus is dependent on Rad52, but not Rad51.
source: This observation is consistent with a previous study showing that spontaneous Holliday junction formation within the rDNA locus is dependent on Rad52, but not Rad51 (Zou and Rothstein, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zou and Rothstein, 1997.

claim: Rad52 may have a function independent of Rad51 and strand annealing at the rDNA locus.
source: Taken together, the evidence suggests that Rad52 may have a function independent of Rad51 and strand annealing at the rDNA locus.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the experimental data and previous studies.

claim: Spontaneous DSB rate can be estimated by the rate of cell death in a rad52∆ mutant, which cannot repair DSBs.
source: Spontaneous DSB rate can be estimated by the rate of cell death in a rad52∆ mutant, which cannot repair DSBs (Coïc et al., 2008; Mehta and Haber, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Coïc et al., 2008 and Mehta and Haber, 2014.

claim: A single unrepaired DSB is sufficient to kill a rad52 mutant cell.
source: A single unrepaired DSB is sufficient to kill a rad52 mutant cell (Weiffenbach and Haber, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Weiffenbach and Haber, 1981.

claim: The mortality rate of the rad52∆ strain was found to be 12% per cell division.
source: Thus, we used the mortality rate of our rad52∆ strain to estimate the rate of spontaneous DSB formation, which we found to be 12% per cell division (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is based on experimental data described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Using direct-repeat recombination assays to detect unequal SCR events, one quarter of spontaneous (two of eight recombinants) and one third of X-ray-induced (four of 12 recombinants) SCR events were found to be accompanied by a crossover.
source: Using direct-repeat recombination assays to detect unequal SCR events, one quarter of spontaneous (two of eight recombinants) and one third of X-ray-induced (four of 12 recombinants) SCR events were found to be accompanied by a crossover (Jackson and Fink, 1981; Kadyk and Hartwell, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jackson and Fink, 1981 and Kadyk and Hartwell, 1992.

claim: If all spontaneous SCE events are the result of DSB repair, the rate of spontaneous SCE should be 3–4%.
source: Therefore, if all spontaneous SCE events are the result of DSB repair, the rate of spontaneous SCE should be 3–4%.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the DSB rate and the proportion of SCR events that result in crossovers.

claim: 20% (43 out of 218, 95% CI [15%, 26%]) of wild-type Strand-seq libraries have at least one SCE not at the rDNA locus.
source: In contrast to this 3–4% upper limit, we find that 20% (43 out of 218, 95% CI [15%, 26%]) of wild-type Strand-seq libraries have at least one SCE not at the rDNA locus.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data.

claim: A DSB in the rDNA locus can be repaired by single-strand annealing in the absence of Rad52 due to the highly repetitive nature of the locus.
source: We exclude SCE events that map to the rDNA locus because a DSB in the rDNA locus can be repaired by single-strand annealing in the absence of Rad52 due to the highly repetitive nature of the locus (Ozenberger and Roeder, 1991).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ozenberger and Roeder, 1991.

claim: Cells lacking both Sgs1 and the structure-specific endonuclease Mus81 are inviable, but this lethality can be suppressed by mutations in the RAD52 epistasis group.
source: For example, cells lacking both Sgs1 and the structure-specific endonuclease Mus81 are inviable, but this lethality can be suppressed by mutations in the RAD52 epistasis group (i.e. RAD51, RAD52, RAD54, RAD55, and RAD57), indicating that mus81∆ sgs1∆ synthetic lethality is due to a toxic recombination intermediate (Fabre et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fabre et al., 2002.

claim: mus81∆ sgs1∆ synthetic lethality is due to a toxic recombination intermediate.
source: For example, cells lacking both Sgs1 and the structure-specific endonuclease Mus81 are inviable, but this lethality can be suppressed by mutations in the RAD52 epistasis group (i.e. RAD51, RAD52, RAD54, RAD55, and RAD57), indicating that mus81∆ sgs1∆ synthetic lethality is due to a toxic recombination intermediate (Fabre et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to Fabre et al., 2002.

claim: The toxic recombination intermediate in mus81∆ sgs1∆ cells cannot be initiated by a DSB.
source: Since Rad52 is required for the repair of DSBs, Fabre and colleagues argued that the toxic recombination intermediate cannot be initiated by a DSB.
evidence: This is an inference based on the role of Rad52 in DSB repair.

claim: Cells lacking Top3 or Rmi1 grow very poorly, but this slow growth can be suppressed by mutations in SGS1 or the members of the RAD52 epistasis group.
source: Similarly, cells lacking Top3 or Rmi1 grow very poorly, but this slow growth can be suppressed by mutations in SGS1 or the members of the RAD52 epistasis group, supporting a model where Rad52 and Sgs1 function in a pathway to repair a spontaneous non-DSB lesion, in the process creating a toxic recombination intermediate requiring Top3 and Rmi1 to resolve (Gangloff et al., 1994; Shor et al., 2002; Chang et al., 2005; Mullen et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Rad52 and Sgs1 function in a pathway to repair a spontaneous non-DSB lesion, in the process creating a toxic recombination intermediate requiring Top3 and Rmi1 to resolve.

claim: rad52 class C mutants, which are defective in Rad52-mediated strand annealing and spontaneous SCE, cannot suppress mus81∆ sgs1∆ synthetic lethality or rmi1∆ slow growth.
source: Unlike rad51∆ and rad52∆, which can suppress the synthetic lethality of mus81∆ sgs1∆ and the slow growth of rmi1∆ (Fabre et al., 2002; Chang et al., 2005), we find that rad52 class C mutants, which are defective in Rad52-mediated strand annealing (Shi et al., 2009) and spontaneous SCE (Figure 2A and B), cannot suppress either phenotype (Figure 4).

claim: The DNA lesion(s) that cause mus81∆ sgs1∆ synthetic lethality and rmi1∆ slow growth are different than the DNA lesion(s) that cause spontaneous SCE in wild-type cells.
source: These findings indicate that the DNA lesion(s) that cause mus81∆ sgs1∆ synthetic lethality and rmi1∆ slow growth are different than the DNA lesion(s) that cause spontaneous SCE in wild-type cells, and that HR is important to repair multiple types of endogenous DNA damage.

claim: HR is important to repair multiple types of endogenous DNA damage.

claim: The majority of spontaneous SCE events in wild-type cells are not the result of DSB repair.
source: In this study, we have used Strand-seq to measure SCE genome-wide in individual yeast cells. We provide evidence that the majority of spontaneous SCE events in wild-type cells are not the result of DSB repair.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the experimental data.

claim: While the strand annealing activity of Rad52 is important for spontaneous SCE, it is not in other noted instances of spontaneous HR, indicating that there must be at least two types of endogenous non-DSB lesions processed by HR.

claim: These lesions could be single-stranded nicks or gaps, as proposed in many of the original models for HR.

claim: It is well known that single-stranded gaps can initiate recombination in Escherichia coli.
source: Indeed, it is well known that single-stranded gaps can initiate recombination in Escherichia coli (Persky and Lovett, 2008) and that fork collapse at the polar replication fork barrier RTS1 in Schizosaccharomyces pombe induces HR-dependent replication restart from a single-stranded gap (Lambert et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Persky and Lovett, 2008.

claim: It has been estimated that a single cell has on average 3.6 Holliday junctions and one DSB within the rDNA array per cell cycle.

claim: The mortality rate of CCY193 (rad52∆) cells is 13.3% (95% CI [9.9%, 17.4%]).
